title: Does a shadow-normalized evolutionary-activity measure rank Sayama's Hash Chemistry above its random-fitness control, and then read evoloop as bounded?
summary: Sayama (Artificial Life 25(2):104-116, 2019, doi:10.1162/artl_a_00283; preprint arXiv:1806.06628) built Hash Chemistry, where a hash function gives a consistent fitness to entities of any order. In it, the cumulative number of unique types of higher-order entities that self-replicate grows almost linearly, with no apparent bound within 2000 steps. Sayama notes that the density limit keeps the set strictly finite, so this is an approximated demonstration. Random-fitness controls fall short. With uniform U[0,1] fitness every run went extinct early. With biased U[0.2,1] fitness, redrawn at each evaluation, novel higher-order types still accumulated, but at only about one third of the hash rate. The control therefore shows reduced novelty growth, not zero. The C:open-ended route asks for a novelty measure that does not saturate, but the collective has no known-positive system to calibrate one against. de Pinho & Sinapayen (arXiv:2603.01701, 2026) found raw total cumulative activity unbounded in 8 of 20 ToLSim runs, while the shadow-normalized total and median activity stayed bounded and new activity stayed null. A measure qualifies only if its shadow-normalized activity (Bedau's neutral-model normalization, GECCO-99 Workshop Program, pp. 34-37) and its new activity separate hash from the biased control by more than the raw roughly 3x novelty-count gap alone would give. Citation fix for source 1: Sayama, H.
